name: Vera Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time today. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, and nothing goes out under your name. Could you start by walking me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior solicitor at a mid-size firm in a regional city that mainly advises family businesses: bakeries, builders, a couple of car dealerships, a printing firm that's on its third generation. I do supplier contracts, employment contracts, and I help on succession, which is handing the business from parents to children. A normal day is drafting, calls with owners who ring at seven in the morning, and visiting a client on site once a week. I use AI tools every day, for drafts, for checking employment rules, for comparing contract versions.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what's still hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the owners. They've built something with their own hands and they want plain answers. What's hard is that I'm still learning the law properly, especially the tax on succession, and the partner I work for, Mr Laurent, catches mistakes I should have spotted. The tools make me faster, but they don't stop me missing what I don't know yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, people can stop panicking and get back to work. The tools are useful, they just aren't a revolution. I'd probably say that on a business forum I post on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, nothing much changes for me. I've got over a year of savings and a small flat I rent out, and family businesses always need a lawyer they trust. I'd keep using the tools and focus on learning succession tax properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going, keep using the tools daily, and ask Mr Laurent to put me on more succession files. I'd look at buying a second rental flat in the next year or two. And I'd do the tax course in the autumn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's a normal, steady world, which I'm happy with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use the tools daily. What would change if they stopped improving?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. I'd still be faster than I would be without them. My real edge would have to come from knowing the law and the clients, which is how it always was.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything else on your mind about work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly my own gaps, the tax especially. And that Mr Laurent is sixty-two and the firm hasn't said who takes over his clients. That's an opportunity if I'm good enough by then.

I'd post on a **business forum** that the tools help but aren't a revolution.
think: Over a year of savings and a **rental flat** keep me secure.
do: Ask my boss Mr Laurent for more **succession files**.
Look at buying a **second rental flat** in a year or two.
Do the **succession tax** course in the autumn.
S0.quote: Family businesses always need a lawyer they trust.
fieldNote: She's **secure**, with savings and a rental flat, so the plateau is comfortable.
She sees her partner's **retirement** as an opening.
She uses AI daily but knows her **knowledge gaps** are the real issue.

steps.text: Take on more family business succession files
Look into buying a second rental flat within two years
Take the succession tax course this autumn

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a chance for small businesses to get good legal help at a fair price. I'd say it on the forum and to clients. At work I'd push us to use the tools properly instead of pretending they don't exist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm a bit uneasy. I'll be fine, because I'm good with the tools, but the firm's partners are slow. If the firm loses clients to cheap online services, juniors go first, even the quick ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pitch Mr Laurent a fixed-fee package for family businesses: contracts, staff handbook and a yearly check-up, done with AI and checked by a lawyer. If he said no, I'd think about setting it up myself in a year or two. I'd keep my savings where they are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more excited than worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the family businesses still need your firm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For the hard stuff, yes. Succession, disputes, selling the business, those need someone who knows the family. The simple contracts, they'll get from a website.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does your rental flat change how you see this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. It's income that doesn't depend on law. It means I can take a risk on starting something without worrying about the bills.

fieldNote: Her own skills feel safe, but the **firm's slowness** worries her.
She'd **build a product** rather than wait to be squeezed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shock, and that businesses and families need to be ready to stand on their own feet. I'd warn clients to get their succession sorted now. I wouldn't call for big government schemes, but I'd want sensible rules.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my job as a junior lawyer is gone in a year or two. If the AI knows succession tax better than my boss, there's no reason to pay me. What might last is being the trusted person who helps a family decide, and that's more about relationships than law.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd leave and start my own small practice in the first six months, mostly AI with me as the person who sits with the family. I'd buy the second flat now, while prices are still normal. If the practice didn't work, I'd look at joining one of my client businesses, maybe running their admin side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'm not frightened of change, but two years is fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your own practice survive this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe for a while, if I'm cheap and trusted. But other people would have the same idea, and the AI would get better at the trust part too. I'd give it two or three years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the business owners you advise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sort out who takes over the business now, while you can still choose. Don't leave it to chance. And get your contracts in writing, because the world's about to move fast.

I'd warn clients to **sort succession** now and ask for sensible rules.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time to prepare, so businesses should start now. I'd write about it on the forum and tell clients. At work I'd push for the firm to change its model.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years suits me. I'd get two or three years of proper training from Mr Laurent, learn succession inside out, and take over some of his clients. Then I'd go out on my own before AGI arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the firm for two or three years, using AI on everything and taking on Mr Laurent's clients as he steps back. I'd buy the second flat in year one. Then I'd start my own practice around 2029 with a client list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but confident. It's a timeline I can work with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's different about five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go out on my own with clients who already know me, instead of rushing. With two years I'd be guessing. With five I'd have a proper plan and a name.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think should carry the cost of this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The businesses and families themselves, mostly, with some help from banks and the market. I don't think the government should pay for everyone. But I'd want them to keep the rules simple so small firms can adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so let's get on with it. I'd be upbeat on the forum. At work I'd say this is our chance to become the firm every family business in the region trusts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, this is a good picture for me. Ten years is enough to become a proper succession lawyer, take over clients and build my own practice. The thinking side of law goes in 2036. By 2036 I'd be running a business, not just doing legal work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the firm for four or five years and learn everything I can. I'd use the tools daily and buy the second and maybe third flat. Then I'd open my own practice or take over part of the firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Quite excited, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is a long runway. What would you build?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A small practice that looks after maybe fifty family businesses, using AI for the drafting and me for the decisions and the kitchen-table talks. And a few rental flats, so I'm not relying on law alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does any of this change your personal plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. I'd like a family of my own one day, and ten years means I could plan for it without everything shifting under me. That matters more to me than people think.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because there's no time to build a client list. What would help is simple rules so small practices can start easily, and families and businesses getting their own houses in order rather than waiting for help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe whether I'm too confident. I might be. But I'd rather bet on myself than wait to see what happens.
